doc.title: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack") Interview, 1959-07-01
doc.interviewee: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack")

title: Punch Miller traveling with the company and his drinking
summary: Billy says Punch was taken on, traveled everywhere and lived with them in Chicago. They fired him after he slept in the pit in Texarkana, then hired him again, buying him a trumpet. Allen gives his later life.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: We were talking about these towns going through like that. Now Punch, when he came into the Orleans, he played around with us. But they didn't recognize him so much because he hadn't been in the Orleans too long. And so he kind of palled around with us because we always accepted any performers, musicians, you know, and fix meals so they could have. And so he got to like us and when we had room for him, we took him on and carried him around with us for a while. He traveled with you then too?

Yes, he did. Because this record that you made, I think on the record label, it says recorded in New Orleans. So I thought maybe he didn't go out of the city with you. Oh, yes. He traveled with us. He went everywhere.
And then here he lived with us. Oh, here in Chicago. Yes. He lived right in the house with us.

But some of the records we made though were made in New York and Clarence Williams played for us. He happened to be there. Yes. He wasn't traveling with us at that time. But once we were here and needed a trumpet player and punch, we got left down south or something. Oh, he turned out to be a kind of boozer. That's what it was. And we had to let him go.
Oh, I shouldn't say that. Well, we won't play that part for you. I'll just play the first part. But anyway, he...
I know I've heard that about him too, that part. But he doesn't drink now. He's three with that forever.

Well, that's what ruined his health anyway. We used to talk to him. Anyway, we left him. We were playing Texarkana, Texas. And he went to sleep in the pit. And that was too much. I was trying to play the show. He didn't. He'd bring his head. Sure didn't.
Tell him, all right, we're ready.

So when we got up here, we found he was in Houston, Texas. And we wired him. And he sent a wire back, said he'd like to come, but he didn't have a trumpet. So I told him, come on empty hands. We give him anyway. And we got here. I had a trumpet for him. I bought one hour, a pawn shop. And he stayed with us a long time after that. He's been right here in this house every time. He's a real meal with us. He'll be glad to hear from you.

And then we just got to, he writes to us all the time. Because he can always find us, but we can't find him. Yes, that's right. Because we have one address, you see. But he's a fine fellow, Punch. Oh, yes.

I've known him now just three years. I never could find him in the years I used to travel around. He was with a carnival. And I could never find him. He wasn't in Chicago when I'd come through here. Mm-hmm. But he came back to New Orleans about almost three years ago now.

And he's been working there sometimes as a musician. He had other jobs too. But now he'll be on the Social Security. He'll be able to get a pension from the Army too. He was in the Army, you know. Yes, yes.
He certainly was. He certainly was in the Army.
